observed.title: Reading data and evaluating evidence
prompts: At Library A, 24 of 80 workshop participants finished a project. At Library B, 30 of 120 finished. Which library has the higher observed completion percentage?
A club's participation rate rises from 40% to 50%. Which statement correctly separates the percentage-point change from the relative percentage increase?
Service Cedar reports 3 late deliveries, and Service Elm reports 6. No total delivery counts are given. What can these counts alone establish about their late-delivery rates?
Five fictional waiting times, in minutes, are 4, 5, 5, 6 and 30. What are their arithmetic mean and median?
In the ordered waiting times 4, 5, 5, 6 and 30 minutes, replace only 30 with 90. What happens to the mean and median?
Twelve students read an arithmetic mean of 5 pages each. Three other students read an arithmetic mean of 20 pages each. What is the arithmetic mean across all 15 students?
On the same 100-point test scale, Group A's mean moves from 40 before a workshop to 60 after it. Group B's mean moves from 70 to 80. What are the observed increases in group means?

Two methods are used by beginners and experienced participants. Method A succeeds for 20 of 80 beginners and 18 of 20 experienced participants. Method B succeeds for 2 of 10 beginners and 72 of 90 experienced participants. Which statement matches these counts?
One group records the values 10, 10, 10 and 10. Another records 0, 0, 20 and 20 in the same units. Which comparison is correct?
A newsletter invites readers to reply voluntarily about a new bus timetable. Of the 200 people who reply, 180 say it is useful. What does the calculated 90% directly describe?

Eighty volunteers are randomly assigned, 40 each, to interface A or B. They perform the same task, and completion time is recorded for everyone. What does random assignment principally help accomplish?

Students choose whether to join a study group. Those who join average 75 on a test; those who do not average 65. No earlier achievement or other differences are measured. Which conclusion is supported by this design alone?

observed.title: Reading data and evaluating evidence — RecallWeave
observed.subject: FIELD NOTES / LOCAL DECK

optionOrder: A: 10 points; B: 20 points.
A: 40 points; B: 70 points.
A: 20 points; B: 10 points.
A: 20 points; B: 20 points.
presentations.selectedText: A: 20 points; B: 10 points.
presentations.expectedCorrectText: A: 20 points; B: 10 points.
presentations.explanation: Subtract each group's own starting mean: A increases by 60 - 40 = 20 points, and B by 80 - 70 = 10. B's higher final mean is a different comparison. These before-and-after means alone do not establish what would have happened without the workshops.
presentations.transfer: Write separate sentences describing the final-score comparison and the change-score comparison. What evidence is still missing for a causal claim?

optionOrder: The methods have equal success rates within both experience groups.
A has the higher success rate overall and within each experience group.
B has the higher success rate overall and within each experience group.
A is higher within each experience group; B is higher when all participants are pooled.
presentations.selectedText: A is higher within each experience group; B is higher when all participants are pooled.
presentations.expectedCorrectText: A is higher within each experience group; B is higher when all participants are pooled.
presentations.explanation: For beginners, A is 20/80 = 25% and B is 2/10 = 20%. For experienced participants, A is 18/20 = 90% and B is 72/90 = 80%. Pooled rates reverse: A is 38/100 = 38%, while B is 74/100 = 74%. B's group contains a much larger share of experienced participants. Different group mixtures can reverse an aggregate comparison; none of these counts alone establishes a causal method effect.
presentations.transfer: If both methods were summarized using an equal 50% weight for beginners and experienced participants, what rate would each method receive? Why must the weighting rule be stated?

optionOrder: Mean 10 minutes; median 6 minutes.
Mean 5 minutes; median 10 minutes.
Mean 10 minutes; median 5 minutes.
Mean 6 minutes; median 5 minutes.
presentations.selectedText: Mean 10 minutes; median 5 minutes.
presentations.expectedCorrectText: Mean 10 minutes; median 5 minutes.
presentations.explanation: The sum is 50 minutes, so the arithmetic mean is 50/5 = 10 minutes. The values are already ordered, and the third of five values is 5, so the median is 5 minutes. The long wait raises the mean without changing which observation occupies the middle.
presentations.transfer: If you had to describe both the usual wait and the long delay, what information would you report beyond a single average?

optionOrder: The mean rises to 22 minutes; the median stays at 5 minutes.
The mean rises to 22 minutes; the median rises to 17 minutes.
The mean stays at 10 minutes; the median stays at 5 minutes.
The mean stays at 10 minutes; the median rises to 22 minutes.
presentations.selectedText: The mean rises to 22 minutes; the median stays at 5 minutes.
presentations.expectedCorrectText: The mean rises to 22 minutes; the median stays at 5 minutes.
presentations.explanation: Increasing one value by 60 raises the five-value sum from 50 to 110. The new mean is 110/5 = 22, an increase of 12 minutes. The ordered middle value is still 5. This example shows why changing an extreme value can affect the mean more than the median.
presentations.transfer: Change only the largest of seven ordered values without moving it below another value. Which middle observation determines the median before and after?

optionOrder: The chance that a different voluntary poll will also report exactly 90%.
The share of these respondents who say the timetable is useful.
The share of all city residents who find the timetable useful.
The share of nonrespondents who would find the timetable useful.
presentations.selectedText: The share of these respondents who say the timetable is useful.
presentations.expectedCorrectText: The share of these respondents who say the timetable is useful.
presentations.explanation: The observed fraction is 180/200 = 90% of the people who replied. The invitation did not randomly sample all residents, and choosing to respond may relate to the opinion being measured. More replies from the same voluntary process do not guarantee that its respondents represent everyone.
presentations.transfer: Consider an unweighted voluntary-response poll. Name its target population, the people invited and the people who responded. If the recruitment method or any group is unstated, say what is missing. Which group does its reported respondent percentage directly describe?

optionOrder: Make the volunteers a random sample of all possible interface users.
Prevent baseline traits from systematically deciding the assigned interface.
Ensure that any difference in task time cannot arise through chance variation.
Ensure every baseline trait is exactly balanced in this particular run.
presentations.selectedText: Ensure every baseline trait is exactly balanced in this particular run.
presentations.expectedCorrectText: Prevent baseline traits from systematically deciding the assigned interface.
presentations.explanation: For this random split, interface allocation is independent of participants' baseline traits by design. It helps avoid systematic allocation differences, but a finite random split can still be imbalanced by chance. It neither turns volunteers into a representative random sample nor eliminates chance variation from the assignment. Study conduct and measurement still matter.
presentations.transfer: Explain the difference between randomly selecting people to join a study and randomly assigning enrolled people to its comparison groups.

optionOrder: Joining the study group raises every student's score by exactly 10 points.
Repeating this voluntary comparison with more students would remove all confounding.
The lack of random assignment proves that study groups cannot affect scores.
The participants scored higher here, but the comparison alone does not establish that joining caused the difference.
presentations.selectedText: The participants scored higher here, but the comparison alone does not establish that joining caused the difference.
presentations.expectedCorrectText: The participants scored higher here, but the comparison alone does not establish that joining caused the difference.
presentations.explanation: The observed difference in group means is 10 points. Self-selection could also separate students by earlier preparation, motivation, available time or other factors. The comparison records an association; it does not identify the effect of joining. It also does not prove that joining has no effect. A stronger design would address alternative explanations rather than only enlarge this comparison.
presentations.transfer: Propose one change to the study that would make the causal question more informative, and state one uncertainty that could still remain.

optionOrder: A: 30%, compared with B: 25%.
B, because six more participants finished.
B: 30%, compared with A: 25%.
Both: 30%, despite different group sizes.
presentations.selectedText: A: 30%, compared with B: 25%.
presentations.expectedCorrectText: A: 30%, compared with B: 25%.
presentations.explanation: Use each library's own participant count: 24/80 = 0.30 and 30/120 = 0.25. B has more completions but a lower completion percentage. These are descriptive results for these groups, not proof that one workshop caused better outcomes.
presentations.transfer: An announcement compares 45 successes with 36 successes. What two additional counts would you request before comparing success rates?

optionOrder: 10 percentage points; a 10% relative increase.
25 percentage points; a 10% relative increase.
25 percentage points; a 25% relative increase.
10 percentage points; a 25% relative increase.
presentations.selectedText: 10 percentage points; a 25% relative increase.
presentations.expectedCorrectText: 10 percentage points; a 25% relative increase.
presentations.explanation: The rate changes by 50% - 40% = 10 percentage points. Relative to the original 40%, the increase is (50 - 40)/40 = 0.25, or 25%. A percentage-point difference and a relative percentage change use different comparisons.
presentations.transfer: A rate falls from 20% to 15%. State the percentage-point decrease and the relative percentage decrease, naming the original-rate denominator.

optionOrder: 8 pages per student.
12.5 pages per student.
20 pages per student.
5 pages per student.
presentations.selectedText: 12.5 pages per student.
presentations.expectedCorrectText: 8 pages per student.
presentations.explanation: The first group reads 12 × 5 = 60 pages in total; the second reads 3 × 20 = 60. Across 15 students, the mean is (60 + 60)/15 = 8 pages. Averaging the two group means to get 12.5 would incorrectly give each group the same weight despite different sizes.
presentations.transfer: When is the unweighted arithmetic mean of two group means equal to the overall mean across all individuals? Give one condition that makes it valid.

optionOrder: Their means are equal, but the second group's range is larger.
The second group's mean is larger, but their ranges are equal.
The first group's mean is larger because none of its values are zero.
Both their means and their individual observed values are equal.
presentations.selectedText: Their means are equal, but the second group's range is larger.
presentations.expectedCorrectText: Their means are equal, but the second group's range is larger.
presentations.explanation: Both sums are 40, and both groups have four values, so both means are 10. The first range is 10 - 10 = 0; the second is 20 - 0 = 20. Identical means can hide different distributions. A center summary does not by itself describe variation.
presentations.transfer: Create a third four-value group with mean 10 and a range between 0 and 20. Check both claims directly.

optionOrder: Elm's rate is higher because it has three more late deliveries.
Cedar's rate is half Elm's because its late count is half as large.
The rates cannot be compared without the total deliveries for each service.
The rates are equal because both services have some late deliveries.
presentations.selectedText: The rates cannot be compared without the total deliveries for each service.
presentations.expectedCorrectText: The rates cannot be compared without the total deliveries for each service.
presentations.explanation: A late-delivery rate divides late deliveries by all deliveries for that service. For example, 3/10 exceeds 6/100, whereas 3/100 is below 6/10. Both examples match the reported late counts. The counts alone therefore do not determine the rate ordering.
presentations.transfer: Construct two possible pairs of total deliveries that give opposite rate rankings while retaining late counts of 3 and 6.

boxes.text: On the same 100-point test scale, Group A's mean moves from 40 before a workshop to 60 after it. Group B's mean moves from 70 to 80. What are the observed increases in group means?

Two methods are used by beginners and experienced participants. Method A succeeds for 20 of 80 beginners and 18 of 20 experienced participants. Method B succeeds for 2 of 10 beginners and 72 of 90 experienced participants. Which statement matches these counts?
AThe methods have equal success rates within both experience groups.
BA has the higher success rate overall and within each experience group.
CB has the higher success rate overall and within each experience group.
DA is higher within each experience group; B is higher when all participants are pooled.
Five fictional waiting times, in minutes, are 4, 5, 5, 6 and 30. What are their arithmetic mean and median?
In the ordered waiting times 4, 5, 5, 6 and 30 minutes, replace only 30 with 90. What happens to the mean and median?
AThe mean rises to 22 minutes; the median stays at 5 minutes.
BThe mean rises to 22 minutes; the median rises to 17 minutes.
CThe mean stays at 10 minutes; the median stays at 5 minutes.
DThe mean stays at 10 minutes; the median rises to 22 minutes.
A newsletter invites readers to reply voluntarily about a new bus timetable. Of the 200 people who reply, 180 say it is useful. What does the calculated 90% directly describe?
AThe chance that a different voluntary poll will also report exactly 90%.
BThe share of these respondents who say the timetable is useful.
CThe share of all city residents who find the timetable useful.
DThe share of nonrespondents who would find the timetable useful.

Eighty volunteers are randomly assigned, 40 each, to interface A or B. They perform the same task, and completion time is recorded for everyone. What does random assignment principally help accomplish?
AMake the volunteers a random sample of all possible interface users.
BPrevent baseline traits from systematically deciding the assigned interface.
CEnsure that any difference in task time cannot arise through chance variation.
DEnsure every baseline trait is exactly balanced in this particular run.

Students choose whether to join a study group. Those who join average 75 on a test; those who do not average 65. No earlier achievement or other differences are measured. Which conclusion is supported by this design alone?
AJoining the study group raises every student's score by exactly 10 points.
BRepeating this voluntary comparison with more students would remove all confounding.
CThe lack of random assignment proves that study groups cannot affect scores.
DThe participants scored higher here, but the comparison alone does not establish that joining caused the difference.
At Library A, 24 of 80 workshop participants finished a project. At Library B, 30 of 120 finished. Which library has the higher observed completion percentage?
BB, because six more participants finished.
A club's participation rate rises from 40% to 50%. Which statement correctly separates the percentage-point change from the relative percentage increase?
A10 percentage points; a 10% relative increase.
B25 percentage points; a 10% relative increase.
C25 percentage points; a 25% relative increase.
D10 percentage points; a 25% relative increase.
Twelve students read an arithmetic mean of 5 pages each. Three other students read an arithmetic mean of 20 pages each. What is the arithmetic mean across all 15 students?
One group records the values 10, 10, 10 and 10. Another records 0, 0, 20 and 20 in the same units. Which comparison is correct?
ATheir means are equal, but the second group's range is larger.
BThe second group's mean is larger, but their ranges are equal.
CThe first group's mean is larger because none of its values are zero.
DBoth their means and their individual observed values are equal.
Service Cedar reports 3 late deliveries, and Service Elm reports 6. No total delivery counts are given. What can these counts alone establish about their late-delivery rates?
AElm's rate is higher because it has three more late deliveries.
BCedar's rate is half Elm's because its late count is half as large.
CThe rates cannot be compared without the total deliveries for each service.
DThe rates are equal because both services have some late deliveries.

observed.subject: FIELD NOTES / LOCAL DECK

optionOrder: A: 40 points; B: 70 points.
A: 20 points; B: 10 points.
A: 10 points; B: 20 points.
A: 20 points; B: 20 points.
presentations.selectedText: A: 20 points; B: 10 points.
presentations.expectedCorrectText: A: 20 points; B: 10 points.
presentations.explanation: Subtract each group's own starting mean: A increases by 60 - 40 = 20 points, and B by 80 - 70 = 10. B's higher final mean is a different comparison. These before-and-after means alone do not establish what would have happened without the workshops.
presentations.transfer: Write separate sentences describing the final-score comparison and the change-score comparison. What evidence is still missing for a causal claim?

optionOrder: The methods have equal success rates within both experience groups.
B has the higher success rate overall and within each experience group.
A is higher within each experience group; B is higher when all participants are pooled.
A has the higher success rate overall and within each experience group.
presentations.selectedText: A is higher within each experience group; B is higher when all participants are pooled.
presentations.expectedCorrectText: A is higher within each experience group; B is higher when all participants are pooled.
presentations.explanation: For beginners, A is 20/80 = 25% and B is 2/10 = 20%. For experienced participants, A is 18/20 = 90% and B is 72/90 = 80%. Pooled rates reverse: A is 38/100 = 38%, while B is 74/100 = 74%. B's group contains a much larger share of experienced participants. Different group mixtures can reverse an aggregate comparison; none of these counts alone establishes a causal method effect.
presentations.transfer: If both methods were summarized using an equal 50% weight for beginners and experienced participants, what rate would each method receive? Why must the weighting rule be stated?

optionOrder: Mean 5 minutes; median 10 minutes.
Mean 10 minutes; median 6 minutes.
Mean 10 minutes; median 5 minutes.
Mean 6 minutes; median 5 minutes.
presentations.selectedText: Mean 10 minutes; median 5 minutes.
presentations.expectedCorrectText: Mean 10 minutes; median 5 minutes.
presentations.explanation: The sum is 50 minutes, so the arithmetic mean is 50/5 = 10 minutes. The values are already ordered, and the third of five values is 5, so the median is 5 minutes. The long wait raises the mean without changing which observation occupies the middle.
presentations.transfer: If you had to describe both the usual wait and the long delay, what information would you report beyond a single average?

optionOrder: The mean stays at 10 minutes; the median stays at 5 minutes.
The mean stays at 10 minutes; the median rises to 22 minutes.
The mean rises to 22 minutes; the median rises to 17 minutes.
The mean rises to 22 minutes; the median stays at 5 minutes.
presentations.selectedText: The mean rises to 22 minutes; the median stays at 5 minutes.
presentations.expectedCorrectText: The mean rises to 22 minutes; the median stays at 5 minutes.
presentations.explanation: Increasing one value by 60 raises the five-value sum from 50 to 110. The new mean is 110/5 = 22, an increase of 12 minutes. The ordered middle value is still 5. This example shows why changing an extreme value can affect the mean more than the median.
presentations.transfer: Change only the largest of seven ordered values without moving it below another value. Which middle observation determines the median before and after?

optionOrder: The chance that a different voluntary poll will also report exactly 90%.
The share of these respondents who say the timetable is useful.
The share of nonrespondents who would find the timetable useful.
The share of all city residents who find the timetable useful.
presentations.selectedText: The share of these respondents who say the timetable is useful.
presentations.expectedCorrectText: The share of these respondents who say the timetable is useful.
presentations.explanation: The observed fraction is 180/200 = 90% of the people who replied. The invitation did not randomly sample all residents, and choosing to respond may relate to the opinion being measured. More replies from the same voluntary process do not guarantee that its respondents represent everyone.
presentations.transfer: Consider an unweighted voluntary-response poll. Name its target population, the people invited and the people who responded. If the recruitment method or any group is unstated, say what is missing. Which group does its reported respondent percentage directly describe?

optionOrder: Make the volunteers a random sample of all possible interface users.
Ensure every baseline trait is exactly balanced in this particular run.
Ensure that any difference in task time cannot arise through chance variation.
Prevent baseline traits from systematically deciding the assigned interface.
presentations.selectedText: Ensure every baseline trait is exactly balanced in this particular run.
presentations.expectedCorrectText: Prevent baseline traits from systematically deciding the assigned interface.
presentations.explanation: For this random split, interface allocation is independent of participants' baseline traits by design. It helps avoid systematic allocation differences, but a finite random split can still be imbalanced by chance. It neither turns volunteers into a representative random sample nor eliminates chance variation from the assignment. Study conduct and measurement still matter.
presentations.transfer: Explain the difference between randomly selecting people to join a study and randomly assigning enrolled people to its comparison groups.

optionOrder: The lack of random assignment proves that study groups cannot affect scores.
Joining the study group raises every student's score by exactly 10 points.
The participants scored higher here, but the comparison alone does not establish that joining caused the difference.
Repeating this voluntary comparison with more students would remove all confounding.
presentations.selectedText: The participants scored higher here, but the comparison alone does not establish that joining caused the difference.
presentations.expectedCorrectText: The participants scored higher here, but the comparison alone does not establish that joining caused the difference.
presentations.explanation: The observed difference in group means is 10 points. Self-selection could also separate students by earlier preparation, motivation, available time or other factors. The comparison records an association; it does not identify the effect of joining. It also does not prove that joining has no effect. A stronger design would address alternative explanations rather than only enlarge this comparison.
presentations.transfer: Propose one change to the study that would make the causal question more informative, and state one uncertainty that could still remain.

optionOrder: B, because six more participants finished.
A: 30%, compared with B: 25%.
Both: 30%, despite different group sizes.
B: 30%, compared with A: 25%.
presentations.selectedText: A: 30%, compared with B: 25%.
presentations.expectedCorrectText: A: 30%, compared with B: 25%.
presentations.explanation: Use each library's own participant count: 24/80 = 0.30 and 30/120 = 0.25. B has more completions but a lower completion percentage. These are descriptive results for these groups, not proof that one workshop caused better outcomes.
presentations.transfer: An announcement compares 45 successes with 36 successes. What two additional counts would you request before comparing success rates?

optionOrder: 10 percentage points; a 10% relative increase.
25 percentage points; a 10% relative increase.
10 percentage points; a 25% relative increase.
25 percentage points; a 25% relative increase.
presentations.selectedText: 10 percentage points; a 25% relative increase.
presentations.expectedCorrectText: 10 percentage points; a 25% relative increase.
presentations.explanation: The rate changes by 50% - 40% = 10 percentage points. Relative to the original 40%, the increase is (50 - 40)/40 = 0.25, or 25%. A percentage-point difference and a relative percentage change use different comparisons.
presentations.transfer: A rate falls from 20% to 15%. State the percentage-point decrease and the relative percentage decrease, naming the original-rate denominator.

optionOrder: 5 pages per student.
20 pages per student.
12.5 pages per student.
8 pages per student.
presentations.selectedText: 12.5 pages per student.
presentations.expectedCorrectText: 8 pages per student.
presentations.explanation: The first group reads 12 × 5 = 60 pages in total; the second reads 3 × 20 = 60. Across 15 students, the mean is (60 + 60)/15 = 8 pages. Averaging the two group means to get 12.5 would incorrectly give each group the same weight despite different sizes.
presentations.transfer: When is the unweighted arithmetic mean of two group means equal to the overall mean across all individuals? Give one condition that makes it valid.

optionOrder: The first group's mean is larger because none of its values are zero.
Both their means and their individual observed values are equal.
The second group's mean is larger, but their ranges are equal.
Their means are equal, but the second group's range is larger.
presentations.selectedText: Their means are equal, but the second group's range is larger.
presentations.expectedCorrectText: Their means are equal, but the second group's range is larger.
presentations.explanation: Both sums are 40, and both groups have four values, so both means are 10. The first range is 10 - 10 = 0; the second is 20 - 0 = 20. Identical means can hide different distributions. A center summary does not by itself describe variation.
presentations.transfer: Create a third four-value group with mean 10 and a range between 0 and 20. Check both claims directly.

optionOrder: Elm's rate is higher because it has three more late deliveries.
The rates are equal because both services have some late deliveries.
The rates cannot be compared without the total deliveries for each service.
Cedar's rate is half Elm's because its late count is half as large.
presentations.selectedText: The rates cannot be compared without the total deliveries for each service.
presentations.expectedCorrectText: The rates cannot be compared without the total deliveries for each service.
presentations.explanation: A late-delivery rate divides late deliveries by all deliveries for that service. For example, 3/10 exceeds 6/100, whereas 3/100 is below 6/10. Both examples match the reported late counts. The counts alone therefore do not determine the rate ordering.
presentations.transfer: Construct two possible pairs of total deliveries that give opposite rate rankings while retaining late counts of 3 and 6.

rows.explanation: For this random split, interface allocation is independent of participants' baseline traits by design. It helps avoid systematic allocation differences, but a finite random split can still be imbalanced by chance. It neither turns volunteers into a representative random sample nor eliminates chance variation from the assignment. Study conduct and measurement still matter.
rows.transfer: Apply the idea: Explain the difference between randomly selecting people to join a study and randomly assigning enrolled people to its comparison groups.
rows.practice: Practice answer · correct on retryPrevent baseline traits from systematically deciding the assigned interface.

rows.prompt: Students choose whether to join a study group. Those who join average 75 on a test; those who do not average 65. No earlier achievement or other differences are measured. Which conclusion is supported by this design alone?
rows.first: The participants scored higher here, but the comparison alone does not establish that joining caused the difference.
rows.correct: The participants scored higher here, but the comparison alone does not establish that joining caused the difference.
rows.explanation: The observed difference in group means is 10 points. Self-selection could also separate students by earlier preparation, motivation, available time or other factors. The comparison records an association; it does not identify the effect of joining. It also does not prove that joining has no effect. A stronger design would address alternative explanations rather than only enlarge this comparison.
rows.transfer: Apply the idea: Propose one change to the study that would make the causal question more informative, and state one uncertainty that could still remain.

rows.prompt: At Library A, 24 of 80 workshop participants finished a project. At Library B, 30 of 120 finished. Which library has the higher observed completion percentage?
rows.first: A: 30%, compared with B: 25%.
rows.correct: A: 30%, compared with B: 25%.
rows.explanation: Use each library's own participant count: 24/80 = 0.30 and 30/120 = 0.25. B has more completions but a lower completion percentage. These are descriptive results for these groups, not proof that one workshop caused better outcomes.
rows.transfer: Apply the idea: An announcement compares 45 successes with 36 successes. What two additional counts would you request before comparing success rates?

rows.prompt: A club's participation rate rises from 40% to 50%. Which statement correctly separates the percentage-point change from the relative percentage increase?
rows.first: 10 percentage points; a 25% relative increase.
rows.correct: 10 percentage points; a 25% relative increase.
rows.explanation: The rate changes by 50% - 40% = 10 percentage points. Relative to the original 40%, the increase is (50 - 40)/40 = 0.25, or 25%. A percentage-point difference and a relative percentage change use different comparisons.
rows.transfer: Apply the idea: A rate falls from 20% to 15%. State the percentage-point decrease and the relative percentage decrease, naming the original-rate denominator.

rows.prompt: Twelve students read an arithmetic mean of 5 pages each. Three other students read an arithmetic mean of 20 pages each. What is the arithmetic mean across all 15 students?
rows.first: 12.5 pages per student.
rows.correct: 8 pages per student.
rows.explanation: The first group reads 12 × 5 = 60 pages in total; the second reads 3 × 20 = 60. Across 15 students, the mean is (60 + 60)/15 = 8 pages. Averaging the two group means to get 12.5 would incorrectly give each group the same weight despite different sizes.
rows.transfer: Apply the idea: When is the unweighted arithmetic mean of two group means equal to the overall mean across all individuals? Give one condition that makes it valid.
rows.practice: Practice answer · correct on retry8 pages per student.

rows.prompt: One group records the values 10, 10, 10 and 10. Another records 0, 0, 20 and 20 in the same units. Which comparison is correct?
rows.first: Their means are equal, but the second group's range is larger.
rows.correct: Their means are equal, but the second group's range is larger.
rows.explanation: Both sums are 40, and both groups have four values, so both means are 10. The first range is 10 - 10 = 0; the second is 20 - 0 = 20. Identical means can hide different distributions. A center summary does not by itself describe variation.
rows.transfer: Apply the idea: Create a third four-value group with mean 10 and a range between 0 and 20. Check both claims directly.

rows.prompt: Service Cedar reports 3 late deliveries, and Service Elm reports 6. No total delivery counts are given. What can these counts alone establish about their late-delivery rates?
rows.first: The rates cannot be compared without the total deliveries for each service.
rows.correct: The rates cannot be compared without the total deliveries for each service.
rows.explanation: A late-delivery rate divides late deliveries by all deliveries for that service. For example, 3/10 exceeds 6/100, whereas 3/100 is below 6/10. Both examples match the reported late counts. The counts alone therefore do not determine the rate ordering.
rows.transfer: Apply the idea: Construct two possible pairs of total deliveries that give opposite rate rankings while retaining late counts of 3 and 6.

Two methods are used by beginners and experienced participants. Method A succeeds for 20 of 80 beginners and 18 of 20 experienced participants. Method B succeeds for 2 of 10 beginners and 72 of 90 experienced participants. Which statement matches these counts?
AThe methods have equal success rates within both experience groups.
BB has the higher success rate overall and within each experience group.
CA is higher within each experience group; B is higher when all participants are pooled.
DA has the higher success rate overall and within each experience group.
Five fictional waiting times, in minutes, are 4, 5, 5, 6 and 30. What are their arithmetic mean and median?
In the ordered waiting times 4, 5, 5, 6 and 30 minutes, replace only 30 with 90. What happens to the mean and median?
AThe mean stays at 10 minutes; the median stays at 5 minutes.
BThe mean stays at 10 minutes; the median rises to 22 minutes.
CThe mean rises to 22 minutes; the median rises to 17 minutes.
DThe mean rises to 22 minutes; the median stays at 5 minutes.
A newsletter invites readers to reply voluntarily about a new bus timetable. Of the 200 people who reply, 180 say it is useful. What does the calculated 90% directly describe?
AThe chance that a different voluntary poll will also report exactly 90%.
BThe share of these respondents who say the timetable is useful.
CThe share of nonrespondents who would find the timetable useful.
DThe share of all city residents who find the timetable useful.

Eighty volunteers are randomly assigned, 40 each, to interface A or B. They perform the same task, and completion time is recorded for everyone. What does random assignment principally help accomplish?
AMake the volunteers a random sample of all possible interface users.
BEnsure every baseline trait is exactly balanced in this particular run.
CEnsure that any difference in task time cannot arise through chance variation.
DPrevent baseline traits from systematically deciding the assigned interface.

Students choose whether to join a study group. Those who join average 75 on a test; those who do not average 65. No earlier achievement or other differences are measured. Which conclusion is supported by this design alone?
AThe lack of random assignment proves that study groups cannot affect scores.
BJoining the study group raises every student's score by exactly 10 points.
CThe participants scored higher here, but the comparison alone does not establish that joining caused the difference.
DRepeating this voluntary comparison with more students would remove all confounding.
At Library A, 24 of 80 workshop participants finished a project. At Library B, 30 of 120 finished. Which library has the higher observed completion percentage?
AB, because six more participants finished.

B25 percentage points; a 10% relative increase.
C10 percentage points; a 25% relative increase.
D25 percentage points; a 25% relative increase.

One group records the values 10, 10, 10 and 10. Another records 0, 0, 20 and 20 in the same units. Which comparison is correct?
AThe first group's mean is larger because none of its values are zero.
BBoth their means and their individual observed values are equal.
CThe second group's mean is larger, but their ranges are equal.
DTheir means are equal, but the second group's range is larger.
